paragraphs: Nonnegative least squares fits a linear model while requiring its coefficients to stay nonnegative. Standard solvers typically treat that restriction as an extra complication. This paper asks what happens when the data are also nonnegative, and shows that the combination provides useful structure that an algorithm can exploit.

The authors introduce an accelerated algorithm based on a primal-dual formulation. Their central theoretical result concerns dimension-independent oracle complexity, a measure of the computational queries required to reach a desired accuracy. For nonnegative data, they obtain multiplicative accuracy with complexity independent of matrix constants. This differs from the stated worst-case behavior of unconstrained least squares, whose corresponding complexity necessarily depends on a matrix quantity and whose accuracy is additive.

The paper also establishes linear convergence by combining its method with adaptive restarting, and demonstrates effectiveness in numerical experiments on large datasets. The contribution is therefore both an algorithm and a sharper account of when nonnegativity helps: the favorable result specifically uses nonnegative data as well as nonnegative coefficients.
neurips-2022-a-fast-scale-invariant-algo.tldr: An accelerated solver exploits nonnegative data to give nonnegative least squares multiplicative accuracy guarantees independent of matrix constants.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether strong theoretical guarantees for learning a neural network also protect it from adversarial examples. Such examples are inputs deliberately altered to exploit a model's weaknesses. Earlier work had established vulnerability in random neural networks, including attacks constructed with a single gradient-ascent step. The authors extend that investigation to networks undergoing lazy training.

Lazy training is a prominent setting in deep learning theory because it supports proofs that neural networks can be learned efficiently. The paper studies overparameterized networks within this setting that also have guarantees of good generalization. Its result shows that these favorable properties can coexist with vulnerability to attacks produced by just one gradient-ascent step.

The finding separates three desirable properties: efficient learning, generalization, and adversarial robustness. In the analyzed setting, the first two do not establish the third. The contribution is specifically about the vulnerability that remains under lazy training; it does not claim that all neural-network training procedures necessarily have the same behavior.
neurips-2022-adversarial-robustness-is-a.tldr: Overparameterized networks in the lazy-training setting can generalize well and be efficiently learnable while remaining vulnerable to one-step adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation uses data collected under one policy to assess another. Estimating a single expected return and learning an entire value function are related but different tasks. Previous guarantees for marginalized importance sampling supported return estimation under realizability, while function estimation had required stronger assumptions. Realizability means that the chosen function classes can represent the relevant targets.

The paper introduces a more flexible regularizer for marginalized importance-sampling objectives. It establishes function-estimation guarantees under realizability and lets the user specify the distribution under which estimation errors matter. This makes the accuracy objective explicit: a learned function can be judged according to a chosen distribution rather than only the weighting implicit in a conventional objective.

The authors also characterize the optimal dual solution that the discriminator class must represent. For value-function learning, that characterization determines the required data coverage. Changing the regularizer can weaken the coverage requirement, and can remove it in an ideal case with strong side information. That last conclusion depends on the additional information, rather than applying to arbitrary datasets.
neurips-2022-beyond-the-return-off-polic.tldr: Flexible regularization enables off-policy function-estimation guarantees under realizability while allowing users to choose how estimation error is weighted.

paragraphs: The paper approaches adversarial defense through the behavior of a dynamical system. Its idea is to make a clean input an asymptotically stable equilibrium: a point toward which nearby disturbed inputs move as the system evolves. If a malicious perturbation starts sufficiently close to that point, the dynamics could reduce the disturbance.

The authors provide a theoretical guarantee with precisely that local condition. When the clean instance is an asymptotically stable equilibrium and the adversarial instance lies in its neighborhood, stability brings the adversarial instance closer to the clean one. They use this result to motivate ASODE, a neural ordinary differential equation whose dynamics change with time.

ASODE places constraints on an associated linear time-varying system to make clean instances act as stable equilibria. The analysis suggests implementing those constraints as regularization terms. Experiments report improved adversarial robustness and performance above state-of-the-art methods. The theoretical protection remains tied to the equilibrium and neighborhood assumptions, while the experiments provide evidence for the resulting implementation.
neurips-2022-defending-against-adversari.tldr: ASODE uses stability-inspired neural dynamics to reduce nearby adversarial perturbations and reports improved robustness in experiments.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning asks an agent to learn across a sequence of tasks. A central challenge is making experience on earlier tasks improve performance on later ones. This paper investigates which parts of a learning system drive that transfer, using Soft Actor-Critic, or SAC, and the continuous-control tasks in Continual World.

The study systematically examines the actor, the critic, exploration, and data. These components cover the agent's action choices, its assessment of actions, how it seeks experience, and the experience available for learning. By examining their contributions to transfer, the authors develop recommendations for modeling choices. They combine their best choices into a method called ClonEx-SAC.

On the Continual World benchmark, ClonEx-SAC reaches an 87% final success rate, compared with 80% for PackNet, described as the benchmark's best existing method. Transfer also rises from 0.18 to 0.54 under the benchmark's metric. These results support the selected combination of design choices in this setting and show improvement in both final task success and measured transfer.
neurips-2022-disentangling-transfer-in-c.tldr: A systematic study of SAC's components produces ClonEx-SAC, improving both final success and measured transfer on Continual World.

paragraphs: Agents that learn to cooperate can settle on arbitrary conventions that their eventual partners do not share. Several conventions may be equally good in isolation yet incompatible when combined. This problem is particularly relevant when agents see only part of the environment and must interpret one another's actions, as in decentralized partially observable decision processes.

The authors introduce an equivariant network architecture that prevents policies from breaking the relevant symmetries. Its purpose is to avoid arbitrary choices among equivalent conventions that undermine coordination. The method also works as a transformation of generic pretrained policies, allowing it to be applied at test time alongside any self-play algorithm.

The paper supplies theoretical guarantees and evaluates the approach in Hanabi. The reported results exceed other symmetry-aware baselines for zero-shot coordination, where agents must coordinate without first training together. The method also improves coordination across a variety of pretrained policies and advances the reported state of the art on that benchmark. This connects architectural symmetry constraints with a practical way to improve already trained agents.
neurips-2022-equivariant-networks-for-ze.tldr: An equivariant architecture reduces incompatible conventions and improves zero-shot coordination, including when applied to pretrained Hanabi policies.

paragraphs: Randomized trials offer strong evidence about treatment effects, but often cover only a narrow population. Observational studies can reach additional groups, although hidden confounding and selection bias may distort their estimates. This paper proposes checking observational estimators against trial evidence before using them to estimate effects for groups absent from the trial.

The method uses validation effects that can be estimated from both randomized and observational data. It attempts to reject observational estimators that fail this comparison, then builds conservative confidence intervals for extrapolated effects using the surviving estimators. Passing validation is therefore part of a screening procedure, rather than a declaration that an observational estimate must be unbiased.

The interval-coverage guarantee assumes that at least one observational estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal for both validation and extrapolated effects. The authors also give conditions supporting asymptotic normality of a doubly robust group-effect estimator when nuisance quantities are learned with flexible machine learning. Semi-synthetic experiments based on IHDP illustrate the approach and show favorable comparisons with standard meta-analysis.
neurips-2022-falsification-before-extrap.tldr: The method screens observational causal estimators against randomized-trial evidence before constructing conservative intervals for populations outside the trial.

paragraphs: Few-shot knowledge-graph completion asks a model to infer an unfamiliar relation from a handful of example triples. Many approaches first train on numerous relation-specific tasks, but assembling those tasks requires human curation. This paper introduces Connection Subgraph Reasoner, or CSR, to make predictions without that curated collection of training tasks.

CSR explicitly models a connection subgraph shared by the support examples and a candidate query. The underlying idea is to identify connecting structure that can explain the examples and apply it to a new case. To adapt CSR to a particular knowledge graph, the authors pretrain it by reconstructing automatically sampled connection subgraphs, creating supervision from the graph itself.

Experiments on NELL, FB15K-237, and ConceptNet support the approach. Even a learning-free version performs competitively with existing methods. Pretraining yields gains of up to 52% on the harder inductive tasks, where entities as well as relations can be unseen during training. The result suggests that learning reusable graph connections can reduce dependence on manually constructed few-shot training tasks.
neurips-2022-few-shot-relational-reasoni.tldr: CSR learns reusable connection subgraphs to reason about new knowledge-graph relations without a curated set of few-shot training tasks.

paragraphs: A point cloud represents a three-dimensional object through a collection of points, while the object's underlying surface can have complicated geometry. Self-attention helps connect distant parts of that collection. The paper argues that conventional attention based on Euclidean dot products does not adequately capture long-range relationships that follow the curved surface represented by the points.

The authors introduce Geodesic Self-Attention, or GSA, as a replacement attention module. It uses a metric on a Riemannian manifold to represent long-range geometric dependencies. The central change concerns how relationships are measured: the module is designed around the object's non-Euclidean structure, including connections along its implicit surface.

The approach reports state-of-the-art performance relative to point-cloud Transformers on object classification, few-shot classification, and part segmentation benchmarks. These tasks cover recognizing complete objects, recognizing them from limited examples, and labeling their parts. Together, the findings support incorporating surface-aware geometry into attention across several point-cloud tasks, rather than treating long-range interaction solely through conventional Euclidean similarity.
neurips-2022-geodesic-self-attention-for.tldr: Geodesic Self-Attention uses manifold geometry to model point-cloud relationships and improves results across classification and segmentation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds representations that distinguish individual examples. Many methods use high-dimensional spaces to make that separation easier. This paper highlights a possible drawback: examples can become so sparsely scattered that meaningful similarities between them are difficult to capture. Separating instances well does not by itself ensure that their relationships remain easy to recognize.

The proposed framework, contrastive learning with low-dimensional reconstruction, or CLLR, adds a regularized projection layer that reduces representation dimensionality. Sparse or low-rank regularization helps adaptively reconstruct the lower-dimensional projection space. The method retains the objective of distinguishing instances while changing the space in which their representations are organized.

The authors prove a tighter error bound for CLLR and report empirical advantages across multiple domains. These findings support low-dimensional contrastive embeddings as a useful design choice for addressing the sparse-scattering issue. The contribution is a way to combine instance discrimination with a more compact representation, backed by both theoretical analysis and experiments, rather than simply maximizing separation in a large feature space.
neurips-2022-learning-contrastive-embedd.tldr: CLLR uses a regularized low-dimensional projection to preserve instance discrimination while better capturing relationships between contrastive embeddings.

paragraphs: Meta-learning trains a model to adapt across tasks, and a separate teacher for each task can improve its generalization. However, obtaining many task-specific teachers can be expensive. This paper proposes Self-improving Momentum Target, or SiMT, which generates teachers from the meta-learner's own training history instead of separately training a target model for every task.

SiMT maintains a momentum network, a temporal ensemble of the meta-learner, and adapts it to individual tasks. These adaptations become targets for knowledge distillation back into the meta-learner. The authors report favorable generalization from the momentum network and its task-specific versions, allowing this feedback process to improve the learner.

They also find that perturbing the meta-learner, for example through dropout, stabilizes improvement by preventing the distillation loss from converging too quickly during meta-training. Experiments show significant gains when SiMT is combined with a range of meta-learning methods in few-shot regression, few-shot classification, and meta-reinforcement learning. The approach thus provides a reusable source of teacher guidance across several kinds of task adaptation.
neurips-2022-meta-learning-with-self-imp.tldr: SiMT creates task-specific teachers from a momentum ensemble of the meta-learner and uses their guidance to improve meta-learning performance.

paragraphs: Randomizing value estimates offers a way for reinforcement-learning agents to explore uncertain actions. Although such methods had appealing empirical performance, their theoretical regret guarantees lagged behind those of optimistic algorithms. This paper shows that a carefully designed randomized approach can achieve nearly optimal worst-case regret in episodic tabular decision processes whose dynamics may vary within an episode.

The construction combines one random seed per episode with a Bernstein-type noise magnitude. Its regret bound scales as H times the square root of SAT, up to logarithmic factors, where H is the planning horizon, S and A count states and actions, and T counts interactions. This matches the stated lower bound apart from logarithmic factors.

The proof introduces a clipping operation that keeps both optimistic and pessimistic estimates occurring with probabilities bounded below by a constant. It also develops a recursive expression for absolute estimation errors. Together, these tools establish that randomized value-function exploration can reach the near-optimal theoretical performance previously obtained only by optimistic algorithms.
neurips-2022-near-optimal-randomized-exp.tldr: Carefully calibrated randomized value functions achieve worst-case regret matching the tabular episodic lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimating symmetric properties of a probability distribution from independent samples. Such properties are unchanged when the possible outcomes are relabeled. Rather than designing a separate estimator for each property, the authors develop a unified plug-in approach based on profile maximum likelihood, or PML, that can support the estimation of various properties.

Their estimator is computationally efficient and sample optimal when the target error epsilon is much larger than n to the power of minus one-third, with n denoting the sample count. Earlier polynomial-time PML-based universal estimators had a threshold of n to the power of minus one-quarter. The new threshold extends sample-optimal estimation into a regime requiring smaller errors.

The authors connect this improvement to an existing theoretical limit. A broad class of universal estimators, including their approach, cannot be sample optimal for every 1-Lipschitz property when epsilon is much smaller than n to the power of minus one-third. The achievement therefore concerns the accuracy range of efficient universal estimation, with the stated lower bound marking a limit to further uniform improvement.
neurips-2022-on-the-efficient-implementa.tldr: An efficient PML-based estimator extends sample-optimal symmetric-property estimation to a higher-accuracy regime approaching a stated universal-estimation limit.

paragraphs: Graph neural diffusion models process information on a graph through dynamics described by partial differential equations. Previous research had investigated their ability to address problems such as over-smoothing and information bottlenecks. This paper turns to a different question: how these models respond when an adversary perturbs the graph's topology, changing its connection structure.

The authors empirically find that graph neural PDEs are intrinsically more robust to these perturbations than other graph neural networks in their comparisons. To explain this behavior, they draw on the stability of the heat semigroup under changes to graph topology. This connects observed robustness to mathematical properties of diffusion as graph structure changes.

The paper also examines several graph diffusion operators and relates them to existing neural PDE models. From this analysis, it proposes a general framework for defining a new class of robust graph networks. The resulting model achieves performance comparable to the state of the art on several benchmarks, supporting diffusion as a route to robustness while retaining competitive predictive performance.
neurips-2022-on-the-robustness-of-graph-.tldr: The paper links graph neural diffusion's observed robustness to diffusion stability and introduces a robust PDE-based graph-network framework.

paragraphs: This paper studies allocating items as they arrive, with each agent required to receive a prespecified fraction of all items. The planner wants to maximize the agents' total value from their allocations. Valuations are assumed to be independent and identically distributed, but their distribution is initially unknown, so the planner must learn while making decisions.

Learning is complicated by strategic reporting. Agents may misstate how much they value an item if doing so improves their allocation. The problem therefore combines uncertainty about preferences with incentives to manipulate the observations used for learning. The proposed mechanism uses online learning while explicitly accounting for these strategic incentives.

The authors establish approximate Bayesian incentive compatibility, a qualified incentive guarantee rather than an assertion that manipulation is impossible. When all agents report truthfully, they also guarantee sublinear regret for each agent's utility relative to the optimal offline allocation policy. Sublinear regret means that this cumulative utility gap grows more slowly than the number of arriving items, making the per-item gap diminish as the sequence grows.
neurips-2022-online-allocation-and-learn.tldr: An online allocation mechanism learns unknown valuations while providing approximate incentive compatibility and sublinear individual regret under truthful reporting.

paragraphs: Novel object captioning involves describing images whose objects lack ground-truth training captions. Without those captions, the model cannot directly use the usual caption-supervision objectives for the novel images. This paper proposes Paraphrasing-to-Captioning, or P2C, a two-stage framework that uses rewriting as a heuristic way to improve the generated descriptions.

In the first stage, the captioning model learns paraphrasing from a language model pretrained on text alone. This expands its available vocabulary and improves linguistic fluency. In the second stage, it paraphrases its own captions using fidelity and adequacy objectives intended to keep the description aligned with the image and sufficiently informative about its visual content.

Because reference captions are unavailable for the novel-object images, image-text association modules provide guidance for these caption characteristics. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on nocaps and COCO Caption. The authors also replace the language and cross-modal association models to test the framework's flexibility. The findings support combining language-based rewriting with visual guidance to learn captions beyond the available paired annotations.
neurips-2022-paraphrasing-is-all-you-nee.tldr: P2C combines language-model paraphrasing with image-text guidance to improve captioning for objects without ground-truth training captions.

paragraphs: Synthetic images offer a way to train image representations while avoiding some concerns associated with real images, including privacy and bias. However, prior approaches relied on a small set of carefully designed image generators. Creating those generators requires expertise, which makes expanding the variety of training images difficult.

This paper proposes a dataset of twenty-one thousand image-generating programs. Each program is a short code snippet that produces a diverse collection of synthetic images. The snippets are easy to modify and execute quickly with OpenGL. The approach broadens the collection of generative processes available for training, rather than relying on only a handful of curated processes.

The dataset supports both supervised and unsupervised representation learning. The authors report that it reduces the gap between pretraining on real images and procedurally generated images by 38%. This is a reduction in the gap, not a claim that synthetic pretraining fully matches real-image pretraining. The result supports large collections of procedural programs as a useful source of image-training diversity.
neurips-2022-procedural-image-programs-f.tldr: A dataset of 21,000 image-generating programs reduces the reported representation-learning gap between procedural and real-image pretraining by 38%.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning often limits expected cumulative cost while maximizing expected reward. An average-cost limit, however, does not guarantee that the probability of exceeding a particular cost threshold stays below a target. This paper addresses that outage probability directly through a framework called Quantile Constrained Reinforcement Learning, or QCRL.

QCRL constrains a quantile of the cumulative-cost distribution. The authors establish the relevant quantile constraint as a necessary and sufficient condition for satisfying the outage constraint. They also tackle the difficulty of applying policy-gradient ideas to a quantile and derive theoretical results for approximating its gradient, making the distributional constraint usable in policy optimization.

Combining these results with a Lagrange multiplier yields Quantile Constrained Policy Optimization, or QCPO. Its implementation uses distributional reinforcement learning and the Large Deviation Principle to estimate cost quantiles and tail probabilities. The implemented algorithm satisfies the outage-probability constraint after training. The stated result concerns the trained policy, rather than guaranteeing that the constraint holds throughout the training process.
neurips-2022-quantile-constrained-reinfo.tldr: QCRL optimizes policies using cost-quantile constraints to control outage probability, with its QCPO implementation satisfying the constraint after training.

paragraphs: Kernel k-means is a clustering method whose computational demands motivate compressed approximations. This paper studies randomized sketches, which provide smaller representations for the clustering computation. The authors ask whether these approximations can reduce computational work while preserving the statistical accuracy associated with exact kernel k-means.

They propose a unified framework covering sub-Gaussian sketches, randomized orthogonal system sketches, and Nyström kernel k-means. Their excess-risk analysis establishes a state-of-the-art bound using only a fraction of the computations. In particular, they show that a sketch dimension on the square-root-of-n scale, expressed as an Omega requirement, suffices to obtain the same accuracy as exact kernel k-means, where n is the sample count.

The result makes the tradeoff between compression and statistical quality explicit across several sketching approaches. Matching accuracy here refers to the analyzed statistical performance, rather than requiring identical cluster assignments. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets validate the theoretical analysis. Together, the framework and evidence support randomized compression as a way to make kernel clustering computationally cheaper without sacrificing its stated accuracy.
neurips-2022-randomized-sketches-for-clu.tldr: A unified analysis shows that randomized sketches can preserve kernel k-means accuracy while substantially reducing computation.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning seeks useful information shared across different views of the same data. The paper focuses on the difficulty of using stronger augmentations, which can involve both task-relevant information and nuisance information that hurts generalization. It introduces RényiCL to make contrastive learning more robust when working with these harder views.

The method builds on a variational lower bound for Rényi divergence. A direct use of that approach suffers from high variance and unstable training, so the authors instead construct an objective based on skew Rényi divergence. They provide a theoretical guarantee explaining how estimating the skew divergence supports training stability.

The resulting objectives implicitly combine hard-negative sampling with easy-positive sampling, helping the model select useful features and disregard nuisance features. ImageNet experiments show that RényiCL with stronger augmentations outperforms other self-supervised methods without additional regularization or computational overhead. Experiments on graph and tabular data also show gains over the original contrastive methods, providing evidence that the proposed objective is useful beyond image representations.
neurips-2022-renyicl-contrastive-represe.tldr: RényiCL uses a stable skew Rényi-divergence objective to improve contrastive learning with stronger augmentations and selectively emphasize useful features.

paragraphs: Amodal segmentation aims to recover an object's complete shape, including portions hidden behind something else. A single image may not contain enough evidence, and full-shape labels are difficult to obtain. SaVos addresses both problems by using video, where a region hidden in one frame may become visible in another.

The framework uses visible object parts as supervision for learning complete masks. Its central intuition is that observations across time can explain occluded regions, including when the object deforms, provided that the deformation can be reasonably learned. Alongside priors about known object types, SaVos learns spatial and temporal patterns that could help it generalize to unfamiliar types.

The method reports state-of-the-art performance on the synthetic FISHBOWL benchmark and the real-world KINS-Video-Car benchmark. It also supports test-time adaptation and outperforms existing models after transfer to a new distribution. These findings support video visibility and temporal structure as useful learning signals for completing object shapes, while the possibility of generalizing to unseen types remains a qualified claim.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-amodal-vide.tldr: SaVos learns complete object masks from visible regions across video frames, achieving strong amodal segmentation and transfer results.

paragraphs: An uncertainty estimate for an image is easier to interpret when it concerns a meaningful attribute, such as hair color or an object's location. Generative models can represent such factors in disentangled latent spaces, where separate latent variables encode semantic information. This paper develops uncertainty intervals for those variables, connecting statistical uncertainty to interpretable image characteristics.

The method first uses quantile regression to propose an interval for each latent coordinate. These initial intervals are heuristic, so a calibration step adjusts them to provide coverage of the true latent value for a new input. The paper presents coverage guarantees that apply regardless of the underlying generative model.

The interval endpoints are then passed through the generator to visualize the uncertainty associated with each semantic factor. This lets the output communicate possible variation in meaningful image content, rather than presenting an unexplained numerical score. The authors demonstrate the approach for inverse problems including super-resolution and image completion, reporting principled uncertainty that adapts to the individual input and remains semantically interpretable.
neurips-2022-semantic-uncertainty-interv.tldr: Calibrated intervals in disentangled latent spaces turn uncertainty about semantic image factors into interpretable visualizations with coverage guarantees.

paragraphs: EEG-based systems often struggle to transfer between recording sessions or people without expensive labeled recalibration. This paper addresses that transfer as unsupervised domain adaptation. It builds on tangent-space mapping, a successful approach using the geometry of symmetric positive definite matrices, while seeking representations that work across domains.

The main component is SPD domain-specific momentum batch normalization, or SPDDSMBN. This layer transforms domain-specific SPD inputs into domain-invariant SPD outputs. It enables end-to-end learning of domain-invariant tangent-space models and can be used with multiple source and target domains, as well as online adaptation. The design brings the alignment operation into the learned geometric model.

The authors incorporate the layer into TSMNet, a simple architecture described as intrinsically interpretable. Experiments across six diverse EEG brain-computer-interface datasets report state-of-the-art transfer performance between sessions and between subjects. The findings support combining geometry-aware normalization with tangent-space modeling to address domain shifts, while retaining an interpretable network structure rather than relying on supervised recalibration for each new domain.
neurips-2022-spd-domain-specific-batch-n.tldr: TSMNet uses geometry-aware domain-specific normalization to learn interpretable EEG models that transfer across sessions and subjects.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, collaborating agents must cope with environments that can change rapidly. The paper studies surprise, a quantity intended to describe how much an agent's environment changes. Although surprise-based learning had received attention for single agents, applying it to fast-moving multi-agent interactions remained an open problem.

The authors approach this problem by considering free energy across the whole agent system. A temporal energy-based model estimates surprise, and the learning objective minimizes that estimate over the joint agent distribution. This puts the collective configuration of agents at the center of the objective, rather than considering each agent's surprise only in isolation.

The formulation is theoretically connected to a minimum conjugate-entropy objective and supports convergence toward minimally surprising states. The authors also evaluate the approach on multi-agent tasks requiring collaboration under fast-paced dynamics, reporting empirical support for their theoretical claims. The contribution is a collective, temporally modeled objective for surprise minimization, with both mathematical analysis and collaborative-task experiments supporting the proposed approach.
neurips-2022-surprise-minimizing-multi-a.tldr: A temporal energy-based model estimates and minimizes collective surprise to support multi-agent learning in rapidly changing environments.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a trained model using unlabeled examples from a new domain. A key question is which unsupervised objective should guide those updates. The authors find that meta-learning an adaptation loss produces something close to temperature-scaled prediction entropy for a cross-entropy-trained classifier, but produces a different objective for a classifier trained with squared loss.

They explain this dependence through the training loss's convex conjugate. Under natural conditions, the resulting unsupervised function provides a good local approximation to the supervised loss and recovers the objectives discovered through meta-learning. This yields a recipe for deriving adaptation losses from supervised training losses within a general class.

The method can also be understood as self-training with a particular soft target called a conjugate pseudo-label. Experiments report better performance than other adaptation alternatives across a wide range of benchmarks. For classifiers trained with PolyLoss, the derived objective differs substantially from entropy and outperforms it. The central implication is that the model's original training objective can guide the choice of test-time adaptation loss.
neurips-2022-test-time-adaptation-via-co.tldr: Convex conjugates provide training-loss-specific objectives and pseudo-labels for adapting classifiers to unlabeled test domains.
